sentences.text: As per the version set out by the complainant in his complaint and affidavit, he was having a longstanding friendly relationship with the accused.

The accused also assured the complainant that being a Government Servant, he would easily repay the loan of Rs 35,00,000/- within a year's time.
Relying on their past rapport, the complainant advanced a loan of Rs 35,00,000/- in cash to the accused on 26.02.2013 against a receipt cum promissory note serving as an acknowledgment.
In order to discharge his liability, the accused also issued a post dated cheque i.e. the cheque in question dated 04.02.2014 for the amount of Rs 35,00,000/-.
The complainant presented the cheque to his bank i.e. State Bank of Patiala, Karala, New Delhi and was returned unpaid with the remarks "Funds Insufficient".
Legal demand notice was issued to the accused in regular course, however, he failed to pay the total cheque amount within 15 days thereof and hence the present case.

Legal Position:-
11.

Before proceeding further to reflect upon the defence and evaluation of evidence, the foremost check point is whether the facts averred by the complainant fulfil the basic statutory requirement for constituting an offence under section 138 NI Act.

The accused has admitted receiving the legal demand notice during his statement under Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.9 of 18 section 313 CrPC and has further not disputed that the legal demand notice has been sent on the correct postal address during his cross-examination.

15. Now, I shall consider whether condition number (ii) i.e. the requirement that the cheque in question have been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability is fulfilled or not.
Towards this end, it is apt to discuss that a negotiable instrument including a cheque carries following presumptions in terms of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of the NI Act.

Section 118 of the NI Act provides :
"Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made:
(a) of consideration :- that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed,
negotiated or transferred was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;"
Jasbir Singh vs Ramji Lal on 29 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/154236796/
6 Section 139 of the N.I Act further provides as follows:
"Presumption in favour of holder:- it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability"
Thus, the combined effect of Section 118(a) and Section 139 of Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.10 of 18 NI Act raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability.

Therefore,
existence of condition number (ii) is also presumed against the accused.
16. When the presumption is raised in favour of the complainant, the burden is shifted on the accused to disprove the case of the complainant by rebutting the presumption.
The accused can displace this presumption on the scale of preponderance of probabilities.
Lack of consideration or a legally enforceable debt need not be proved beyond a reasonable doubt as is the general rule in criminal cases.
The accused has to make out a fairly plausible defence which is acceptable to the court.
This the accused can do either by leading his own evidence or by raising doubt /demolishing the material or evidence brought on record by the complainant.

Reliance can be placed on Basalingappa v Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418.
17.

Further, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated.
Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant.

To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist.
The accused may Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.11 of 18 also rely upon circumstantial evidence to shift the burden again on the complainant.

sentences.text: The first and foremost defence of the accused as is apparent from the cross-examination of the complainant is that the financial capacity of the complainant to advance the alleged loan is challenged.
It is trite that in a trial under section 138 NI Act, the complainant is not required to prove his financial capacity at the first instance.

However, the accused has the right to demonstrate that the complainant in a particular case did not have the capacity and therefore, the case of the accused is acceptable which he can Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.12 of 18 do by producing independent materials, namely, by examining his witnesses and producing documents.
It is also open to him to establish the very same aspect by pointing to the materials produced by the complainant himself.
He can further, more importantly, achieve this result through the cross-examination of the witnesses of the complainant.
Reliance can be placed on the recent judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Tedhi Singh v Narayan Dass Mahant (2022) 6 SCC 735.

sentences.text: With this legal proposition in mind, I shall now analyse the record.
20.1. During the cross-examination the complainant stated that his monthly income was around Rs.20,000/- to Rs.30,000/- and his household expenses were also around Rs 25,000/- per month.
His children were also receiving education indicating that they were not contributing to the family income.
20.2. As per the complainant, the loan was advanced out of Rs 40 lacs which he had received on 13.02.2013 as compensation given by the Government for land acquisition.
The complainant has been able to show that he had indeed received such an amount by way of cheque clearing in his bank account.
The complainant has also shown that this amount was withdrawn by him in cash using self cheque.

20.3. However, perusal of the bank passbook of the complainant reveals that this amount of Rs 40 lacs was deposited again by way of two separate cash deposits of Rs 10 lacs and Rs 30 lacs and was Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.13 of 18 promptly transferred by the complainant to some other account (Refer Table 1.1 above).

Relevant excerpts from his testimony are being reproduced hereunder:-
"The entries in my statements of account are correct.

The Rs. 30 lacs deposed in my account on 12.04.2013 were not out of Rs. 40 lacs withdrawn by me in February,
2013.
It was my separate money received from other sources.
I do not remember the source from which I received this amount of Rs. 30 lacs as it was about six years ago.

I do not remember to whom I transferred Rs. 30 lacs on 12.04.2013."
20.4.
In the considered view of this court, Rs 40 lacs is a generational income for a person whose monthly income is in the range of Rs 20,000/- to Rs 30,000/-.
It is almost impossible that a person would not even remember the source from which he received such an amount and the purpose for which he utilized such an amount.
Complainant's response to these questions appears to be a feeble attempt at dodging these questions and concealing material information from this court.

It is also highly probable that the amount Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.14 of 18 Jasbir Singh vs Ramji Lal on 29 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/154236796/
8 of Rs 40 lacs which was withdrawn by the complainant was never advanced to the accused but was redeposited in cash by the complainant to his own bank account.

Given these factors, I am of the view that in the present case the financial capacity of the complainant is not merely doubtful, rather, it has been proved on a scale of preponderance of probabilities that the source of funds as claimed by the complainant himself were circulated back in his own bank account thereby destroying the entire foundation of his claim to be financially capable of advancing the alleged loan to the accused.
21.
There are additional circumstances that suggest the complainant never advanced the alleged sum to the accused.
For instance, the complainant stated that he did not inquire about the business the accused planned to establish for his children, claiming it was not important to him.
This response is wholly unsatisfactory.
According to the complainant, he had advanced a substantial sum of Rs 35 lakhs to the accused for one year without any interest.
It is highly improbable that a prudent person would lend such a significant amount for altruistic reasons without even asking about its intended use.
22. Furthermore, the complainant mentioned that after providing the amount, he never followed up with the accused on how the funds were being utilized, despite the fact that they are neighbours.
This behaviour is inconsistent with that of a prudent person.

23. Additionally, the complainant stated that he lent the money to the Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.15 of 18 accused because he was confident it would be repaid, as the accused was a government employee.

sentences.text: However, he admitted during cross-examination that he knew the accused was a fourth-grade employee working for the MCD.

It is highly unlikely that any prudent person would lend Rs 35,00,000/- to a government employee with a modest income,
expecting that it would be repaid within a year.
24.
I have also considered the argument of Ld. Counsel for the complainant that the complainant has placed on record the promissory note evidencing that the loan was indeed advanced to the accused.

I have also carefully scrutinized the promissory note and I make the following observations:-
24.1.
The accused has denied executing the promissory note.
24.2. During his cross-examination, the complainant stated that he did not know who authored the promissory note, as the document was already filled out by the accused.
He also mentioned that the accused affixed his signatures on the promissory note in his presence.
This testimony suggests that the text was written first, followed by the signatures.
However, upon examining the promissory note, it is evident that space was carefully left around the alleged signatures and thumb impressions of the accused.
This arrangement is only possible if the text was written after the signatures and thumb impressions were obtained.

Therefore, the complainant's Jasbir Singh vs Ramji Lal on 29 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/154236796/
9 testimony Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.16 of 18 regarding the promissory note cannot be believed as a gospel truth.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 24.3. Furthermore, once this court has come to the conclusion that the accused was never having the financial capacity to advance the alleged loan amount, the relevance of the promissory note/receipt pales into insignificance.

25. I have also considered the argument of Ld. Counsel for the complainant that the averment that a blank signed security cheque has been misused is not a valid defence in light of the dictum of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Suresh Chandra Goyal v Amit Singh Crl. LP No. 706/2014 decided on 14.05.2015 and Sheela Sharma v Mahendra Pal Crl LP 559/2015 decided on 02.08.2016.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, in the present case, the accused has been able to create a reasonable doubt about the alleged loan amount being advanced itself and hence, it cannot be said that the cheque represented the crystallised legal liability of the accused on the date of its presentation.

26. For all these reasons, I am of the view that on a scale of preponderance of probabilities, the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him and therefore ingredient no. (ii) has not been established against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Conclusion 27.

In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.17 of 18 above discussion, the court is of the considered view that Sh. Ramji Lal is not guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, he is hereby acquitted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

Also, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the defendant-accused cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof.
Presumption of innocence as a human right needs to be delicately balanced with doctrine of reverse burden contained in section 139 of NI Act.
[Reference can be made to Rangappa v Sri Mohan 2010 SCC OnLine SC 583 and Krishna Janardhan Bhat v Dattatreya G Hegde 2008 (4) SCC 54].
19.
Reliance can be placed on the recent judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Tedhi Singh v Narayan Dass Mahant (2022) 6 SCC 735.
However, in the present case, the accused has been able to create a reasonable doubt about the alleged loan amount being advanced itself and hence, it cannot be said that the cheque represented the crystallised legal liability of the accused on the date of its presentation.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
16. When the presumption is raised in favour of the complainant, the burden is shifted on the accused to disprove the case of the complainant by rebutting the presumption.
The accused can displace this presumption on the scale of preponderance of probabilities.
The accused has to make out a fairly plausible defence which is acceptable to the court.
This the accused can do either by leading his own evidence or by raising doubt /demolishing the material or evidence brought on record by the complainant.
Reliance can be placed on Basalingappa v Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418.
17.
The accused may Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.11 of 18 also rely upon circumstantial evidence to shift the burden again on the complainant.
However, the accused has the right to demonstrate that the complainant in a particular case did not have the capacity and therefore, the case of the accused is acceptable which he can Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.12 of 18 do by producing independent materials, namely, by examining his witnesses and producing documents.
25. I have also considered the argument of Ld. Counsel for the complainant that the averment that a blank signed security cheque has been misused is not a valid defence in light of the dictum of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Suresh Chandra Goyal v Amit Singh Crl. LP No. 706/2014 decided on 14.05.2015 and Sheela Sharma v Mahendra Pal Crl LP 559/2015 decided on 02.08.2016.
opennyai_summary.decision: In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the Ct Case No.29262/2016 Jasbir Singh v Ramji Lal Page no.17 of 18 above discussion, the court is of the considered view that Sh. Ramji Lal is not guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, he is hereby acquitted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
